author: tokenops-maintainers
_note: Fingerprints are taken from CI's scan (nox 1.48.1, pinned in
.github/workflows/security.yml), not from a local scan. A local nox
is a different scanner: 1.35.0 does not report the release.yml:95
statement below at all, and a fingerprint minted by the wrong
version waives nothing in the run that gates the build.
The workflow statements date from the 2026-09-14 suppression
review, when .github/workflows/*.yml stopped being excluded; the
rest from the 2026-10-22 triage that started uploading SARIF to
code scanning. Each binds to one finding by _nox_fingerprint:
scripts/sec-gate.py and scripts/sarif-apply-vex.py both match on
it. Do not pass this file to `nox scan --vex` and read the result
as the triage: nox 1.48.1 matches statements by rule ID alone, so
one AI-006 waiver there hides every AI-006 finding.

statements.impact_statement: ci.yml uploads coverage.out, a Go coverage profile with 7-day retention that is read by the bench gate and by humans. Build-provenance attestation binds a signed claim to an artifact someone downstream installs or executes; nothing consumes this one, and it is never published. The rule is right about release artifacts and this is not one — goreleaser publishes the distributed binaries directly to the release, without upload-artifact.

security.yml uploads findings.json — the scan's own report, 7-day retention, consumed by the summarise step and by anyone reading the run. Attesting a scanner's output to itself adds no verifiable claim: the artifact is diagnostic, not distributed.

id-token: write is mandatory for actions/deploy-pages — it is how the deployment authenticates to GitHub Pages over OIDC instead of a long-lived token. Requesting it is the mitigation the rule would otherwise recommend. The surrounding block is already least-privilege: contents stays read, and pages: write is the only other grant.

nox-remediate.yml runs weekly on a cron; workflow_dispatch exists so a maintainer can run remediation off-schedule when a CVE lands on a Tuesday. Dispatching a workflow requires write access to the repository, so the trigger grants an adversary nothing they would not already have.

pages.yml is path-filtered to web/docs/**, so a docs redeploy after an unrelated change needs a manual trigger or it never runs. Same reasoning as nox-remediate.yml: dispatch requires repository write access.

The concurrency group is keyed on ${{ github.ref }}, so a cancel only ever supersedes an older run of the same ref by a newer commit on that ref. No run of a commit that remains current is cancelled. That this was a considered choice rather than a default is visible one workflow over: pages.yml sets cancel-in-progress: false, because there a cancel could leave a half-published site.

Same ref-scoped concurrency group as ci.yml. A superseded security scan is a scan of a tree that no longer exists; the scan that replaces it covers the tree that does. Findings describe tree state, not history, so nothing is lost by the cancel.

nox-remediate.yml opens dependency-remediation pull requests, which needs contents: write to push the branch and pull-requests: write to open the PR. Those two are the whole permission block. The job body is a single delegation to klarlabs-studio/.github's central workflow, so the privilege is exercised by reviewed org-level code, not by steps defined here.

release.yml creates GitHub releases through goreleaser, which cannot write a release without contents: write. It is the only permission the workflow declares, and the workflow only triggers on v* tags — pushing one already requires write access.

scripts/config-matrix.py is the release's pre-publish harness. It starts the just-built tokenops with subprocess.Popen and an argument LIST ([ARGS.bin, "start", "-c", cfgp]), never shell=True, so no shell parses anything and the environment cannot inject a command. The "tainted" env is the harness's own environment with every TOKENOPS_ variable removed and HOME and XDG pointed at a throwaway directory: the isolation the harness exists to provide. ARGS.bin is the binary the operator running the harness names on its command line.

The same subprocess.Popen call in scripts/config-matrix.py as the waiver above, reported a second time as "proc flows from env_var" (nox 1.48.1 finds both paths locally; CI reports the first). It passes an argument LIST, never shell=True, with the harness's own isolated environment: no shell parses anything, so nothing can be injected.

HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN: snapshot in CI's "Release dry run" is a placeholder, not a credential: goreleaser runs with --snapshot, which never pushes the cask, and its template only needs the variable to exist. The real token comes from secrets.HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN in release.yml only. nox reports it as critical once the team-image steps were removed from the job; same line, same fingerprint as before.

antigravity.go:353 — the http.Transport that sets InsecureSkipVerify talks only to the Antigravity language server on this machine. Its DialContext refuses every address that is not 127.0.0.1, so the skipped verification can only ever apply to a loopback connection; the local server presents a self-signed certificate that has no CA to chain to. No remote peer is reachable through this client.

fmt_recovery_test.go:51 — the constant is 'sk-ant-api03-' followed by repeated 'A's: a synthetic fixture shaped like an Anthropic key so the test can assert that fmt recovery files redact it. It is not, and never was, a credential.
fmt_recovery_test.go:76 — 'sk-ant-api03-' followed by repeated 'B's, the synthetic key the command-line redaction test passes as a flag. Not a credential.
descriptor.go:128 — `PasswordLogin Credential = "password-login"` is an enum value naming a sign-in method, not a password. The detector reads the identifier as a Terraform password field.

groq.go:43 — groqStytchPublicToken is the Groq console's Stytch *public* token ('public-token-live-…'). Stytch public tokens are designed to ship in browser JavaScript and are served in the console's own page; they authorise nothing on their own. It is not a Groq API key.

GO-2026-5932 is the deprecation of golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp itself, so there is no fixed version to move to. No package in this module imports openpgp or its subpackages (git grep finds none), and nox's own applicability check reports the affected package is not linked by this build.
.goreleaser.yaml:126 — github-actions@github.com is the public commit identity of the GitHub Actions bot, used as the Homebrew tap commit author. It is not personal data.

integrations/python/examples/langchain_workflow.py imports langchain_openai, the real PyPI package langchain-openai published by the LangChain project. It is a runnable example, not part of the tokenops_langchain package, which deliberately does not depend on any one model provider; the example's reader installs it alongside an OPENAI_API_KEY. Not a hallucinated package.

assets/brand/make.py is a maintainer-run script that regenerates the logo files; nothing builds, ships or imports it. fontTools is the established fonttools package on PyPI (github.com/fonttools/fonttools), and the script's docstring names it as the requirement. Not a hallucinated package.

verify.go:631 — returns a fixed sentence naming an HTTP status code from a PromptEvent ('upstream HTTP %d failure'). The rule matches the variable name `prompt`; no prompt or response text is read or logged.

checkup.go:98 — fmt.Fprint* writes to the command's own stdout; the rule matches the identifier 'prompt' or the word 'instructions'. It prints a grade and a count of instructions (an integer). No prompt text is logged.

cookie_setup.go:292 and :398 (one line-independent fingerprint) — readSecret/readCopiedRequest print the interactive question shown to the operator (the `prompt` parameter is UI text such as 'Paste the cookie: '), then read the answer without echo. No LLM prompt or response is involved.

dx.go:177 — fmt.Fprint* writes to the command's own stdout; the rule matches the identifier 'prompt' or the word 'instructions'. It prints counts of instructions and sessions. No prompt text is logged.
provider_setup.go:112 — prints a fixed sentence that the daemon re-reads a browser session 'without ever showing a prompt' (a UI prompt). No LLM prompt or response is involved.
provider_setup.go:271 — readLine prints the interactive setup question (the `prompt` parameter is UI text) before reading a line from stdin. No LLM prompt or response is involved.
replay.go:169 — prints the replay selector and the number of prompts replayed (len of a slice). No prompt or response text is logged.

aws_profiles.go:299 — SHA-1 here is a file-naming function, not a security control: the AWS CLI names each SSO cache file ~/.aws/sso/cache/<sha1(session name or start URL)>.json, and tokenops must compute the same name to find the token the CLI cached. No integrity or authenticity decision rests on the hash; changing the algorithm would only stop tokenops finding the file.

eval/testdata/fmtrecall/terraform.plan.txt:26 — a captured `terraform plan` output used as a formatter fixture and fmt recall eval case; 54.1.2.3 is an example public_ip inside that sample text, not configuration anything connects to.

release.yml:31 uploads menubar-app.tar.gz with 1-day retention purely to hand the built bundle from the menubar-app job to the goreleaser job of the same run. The artifact is never published; what users install is the release asset goreleaser uploads, verified by the release's checksums.txt. Attesting an intra-run handoff adds no claim anyone verifies.

nox-remediate.yml:28 — workflow_dispatch lets a maintainer run remediation off-schedule. Dispatch requires repository write access, and the job only opens a pull request that must pass the required checks and review before it reaches main, so an approval environment would gate nothing an attacker could reach. GitHub also does not allow `environment:` on a job that calls a reusable workflow, which is what this job is.

release.yml:154 — id-token: write is mandatory for npm trusted publishing: the npm job authenticates to the registry over OIDC and signs provenance with it, instead of holding a long-lived NODE_AUTH_TOKEN. The grant is scoped to that one job, beside contents: read.
redaction/fuzz_test.go:40 — the fuzz test's list of strings the redactor must never emit: obviously synthetic key-shaped values ('sk-secretsecret…', 'AIzaSyDxxxx…'). Not credentials.
harnesskeys_test.go:54 — expected output rows such as 'sk-ds-env' and 'sk-or-claude': short placeholder values the test plants in fake harness configs. Not credentials.

scanscope_test.go:13 — a macOS temporary-directory path ('-private-var-folders-wz-…-T-worksim-…') used to test scratch-directory detection. The high-entropy segment is the OS's per-user folder hash, not a secret.
bedrock_test.go:23 — AKIDEXAMPLE / wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG+bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY are the example credentials from AWS's published SigV4 test suite, used to check the signer against AWS's known answer.
bedrock_test.go:23 — the same AWS SigV4 test-suite example secret, read by the base64 detector. Published by AWS for exactly this purpose.
bedrock_test.go:25 — the expected SigV4 signature from AWS's published test suite (a hex digest of the example request), not a secret.

web/docs/package-lock.json — mitt is the widely used ~200-byte event emitter (github.com/developit/mitt), pulled in by the VitePress docs toolchain. Its name resembling mqtt is a coincidence of short names, not a typosquat; the locked version resolves from the npm registry with an integrity hash.

security.yml:98 and :103 (one line-independent fingerprint) — continue-on-error is set on the two reporting steps only: applying waivers to the SARIF and uploading it to code scanning. Reporting must never gate the build (an upload from a fork PR has no security-events: write and always fails). The blocking decision is the Critical gate step, which has no continue-on-error, so no security outcome is masked.

pages-redirect.yml — id-token: write is mandatory for actions/deploy-pages: it is how the deployment authenticates to GitHub Pages over OIDC instead of a long-lived token. The block is otherwise least-privilege (contents stays read, pages: write is the only other grant), and the workflow only publishes a static page that forwards the old docs addresses to team.klarlabs.de.

GO-2026-5932 concerns golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp, which is unmaintained by design and has no fixed version. TokenOps imports no openpgp package, and the scan reports the affected package is not linked into this build; x/crypto is present for other packages only.
